01: At 12:01 a.m. MTV goes on the air over film of the first landing on the Moon. Its first music video is 'Video Killed the Radio Star' by the Buggles.
The Mississippi crests at St. Louis at a record 49.6 feet, nearly 20 feet above flood stage. The 52-foot floodwall holds with just over two feet to spare. The river stays in flood until October 7.
02: Andrew Hallidie's Clay Street Hill Railroad makes its first run in San Francisco, a day later than its franchise required: the first successful cable-hauled street railway. Service starts September 1.
About 2:27 a.m. the Japanese destroyer Amagiri cuts PT-109 in two in the Solomon Islands. Two men die. Lt. John F. Kennedy and ten others swim 3.5 miles to a deserted island; rescue comes August 8.
03: At 11:15 p.m. Eastern the nuclear submarine Nautilus, Commander William Anderson, passes under the North Pole: the first vessel to reach it. She crosses beneath the ice in 96 hours.
Radio Shack announces the TRS-80 at a New York press conference: a Z80 computer for $399, or $599 with a 12-inch monitor and a tape recorder. More than 10,000 sell in the first month and a half.
04: On Alexander Hamilton's advice Congress creates the Revenue-Marine: ten cutters to enforce the customs laws. Until 1798 it is the nation's only armed force afloat. In 1915 it becomes the Coast Guard.
05: Agamemnon lands the eastern end of the first Atlantic telegraph cable at Valentia Island, Ireland; Niagara lands the western end at Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, that morning. It fails in September.
06: At 8:15 a.m. the B-29 Enola Gay, flown from Tinian by Col. Paul Tibbets, drops the atomic bomb 'Little Boy' on Hiroshima. By the end of the year 90,000 to 166,000 people there are dead.
Tim Berners-Lee of CERN posts a short summary of his World Wide Web project to the newsgroup alt.hypertext, inviting collaborators. The first website has been up since December.
07: IBM gives Harvard its Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator: Howard Aiken's Mark I, 51 feet long, 765,000 parts, 500 miles of wire. It adds three times a second. Grace Hopper helps program it.
Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft Kon-Tiki smashes onto the reef at Raroia in the Tuamotus, 101 days and 4,300 miles out of Callao, Peru, with a crew of six.
08: At Honesdale, Pennsylvania, Horatio Allen drives the English-built Stourbridge Lion on its first run: the first locomotive operated in the United States. It proves too heavy for the track.
09: The DeWitt Clinton makes its first passenger run on the Mohawk and Hudson Railroad, Albany to Schenectady, in 38 minutes: the first working steam locomotive built for service in New York state.
At 11:02 a.m. the B-29 Bockscar, Maj. Charles Sweeney, drops the atomic bomb 'Fat Man' on Nagasaki; the first target, Kokura, was passed over. 60,000 to 80,000 people die by the end of the year.
10: Missouri is admitted to the Union as the 24th state, a slave state under the Missouri Compromise. The temporary capital is St. Charles; Jefferson City takes over in 1826.
Alexander Graham Bell hears voices sent eight miles over the telegraph line from Brantford to Paris, Ontario. It works only one way, but many sources call it the world's first long-distance call.
11: Actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil receive U.S. patent 2,292,387 for a radio torpedo guidance system that hops between frequencies to defeat jamming. The Navy turns it down.
The Fifteen Guinea Special runs from Liverpool to Carlisle and back behind four engines in turn: British Rail's last main-line passenger train hauled by steam. The steam ban starts the next day.
12: IBM releases the Personal Computer, model 5150, developed in Boca Raton, Florida: an Intel 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 16 KB of memory and PC DOS from Microsoft, starting at $1,565.
13: Eagle Day: the Luftwaffe opens its all-out assault on the Royal Air Force. Germany loses 47 or 48 aircraft; the RAF loses 13 fighters and 11 bombers in the air and 47 planes on the ground.
14: Seven motorcycle races are the first motor racing at Carl Fisher's new Indianapolis Motor Speedway. Car racing follows within days on crushed stone; soon the track is repaved with 3.2 million bricks.
At 7 p.m. in Washington, President Truman announces that Japan has surrendered. The largest crowd in the history of Times Square gathers. The surrender is signed on USS Missouri on September 2.
Just after 4:10 p.m. Eastern a blackout spreads over eight states and Ontario: 55 million people. A power line touched a tree in Ohio, and a software bug had stalled the control room's alarm system.
15: Near Strasburg, Colorado, the Kansas Pacific drives the last spike of the first continuous transcontinental railroad. It is the only all-rail route across the country until 1872.
The Panama Canal is formally opened as the steamship Ancon makes the passage. The 51-mile waterway cost the United States almost $500 million and about 5,600 workers' lives.
Ohio State's Big Ear radio telescope records a strong 72-second signal at 1420 MHz from the direction of Sagittarius. Days later Jerry Ehman writes 'Wow!' on the printout. It has never recurred.
16: Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchange greetings over the new Atlantic cable. Her message runs 98 words. The next morning New York fires a 100-gun salute; that night the city is lit up.
Air Force Capt. Joseph Kittinger steps from a balloon gondola at 102,800 feet, falls for 4 minutes 36 seconds and reaches 614 mph. His jump record stands for 52 years.
17: Robert Fulton's North River Steamboat, later called the Clermont, leaves New York for Albany: 150 miles in 32 hours, with an engine by Boulton and Watt. Steam is shown to pay on the water.
At 11:30 p.m. Hurricane Camille comes ashore at Waveland, Mississippi, as a Category 5 with 175 mph winds and a 24.6-foot surge, the highest then recorded in the continental United States.
The balloon Double Eagle II lands at Miserey, near Paris, 137 hours 6 minutes out of Presque Isle, Maine. Ben Abruzzo, Maxie Anderson and Larry Newman are the first across the Atlantic by balloon.
18: At the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, Asaph Hall finds Phobos, the inner moon of Mars, with the 26-inch refractor, days after finding Deimos. Phobos circles Mars in 7 hours 39 minutes.
19: The Soviet Union launches the dogs Belka and Strelka into orbit with forty mice and two rats. They land the next day: the first animals sent into orbit and returned safely to Earth.
20: At 7 p.m. The New York Times sends a cablegram from its 17th floor: 'This message sent around the world.' Relayed by 16 operators, it travels more than 28,613 miles and is back in 16.5 minutes.
Voyager 2 lifts off on a Titan IIIE, sixteen days before Voyager 1. It becomes the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune, and it enters interstellar space in 2018.
21: A total solar eclipse crosses the United States from the Pacific to the Atlantic, the first to do so since 1918. Totality touches 14 states, with about 2 minutes 38 seconds at Columbia, Missouri.
22: Watched by Queen Victoria, the New York Yacht Club's schooner America beats 15 yachts of the Royal Yacht Squadron around the Isle of Wight. The trophy becomes the America's Cup.
The city of St. Louis votes to secede from St. Louis County and become an independent city. After a recount the separation takes effect in March 1877.
The Cadillac Automobile Company is established from the remnants of the Henry Ford Company, under Henry Leland. It is named for the French explorer who founded Detroit.
23: Lunar Orbiter 1, the first American spacecraft to orbit the Moon, takes the first picture of the Earth from the distance of the Moon.
24: Hurricane Andrew hits Elliott Key, Florida, then Homestead as a Category 5 with 165 mph winds. It destroys 63,500 houses and does $27.3 billion in damage: the costliest U.S. hurricane until Katrina.
Microsoft ships Windows 95, code-named Chicago, with a Start menu, a taskbar and long file names, to the Rolling Stones' 'Start Me Up'. A million copies ship in four days.
25: Paris is liberated. General von Choltitz surrenders the German garrison at 3:30 p.m. at the Hotel Meurice to Leclerc's French 2nd Armored Division, which entered with the U.S. 4th Infantry Division.
Voyager 2 passes about 3,000 miles above the north pole of Neptune, twelve years after launch. No other spacecraft has visited the planet.
Linus Torvalds, 21, a student at the University of Helsinki, tells the newsgroup comp.os.minix he is writing a free operating system: 'just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu.'
26: Experimental station W2XBS in New York televises a major league baseball game for the first time: a doubleheader between the Cincinnati Reds and the Brooklyn Dodgers.
27: Erich Warsitz flies the Heinkel He 178, powered by Hans von Ohain's HeS 3 engine: the world's first aircraft to fly on the thrust of a turbojet. Germany invades Poland days later.
28: The likeliest date of the race between a horse-drawn car and Peter Cooper's Tom Thumb, the first American-built steam locomotive on a common-carrier railroad. The horse wins when a blower belt slips.
Kiichiro Toyoda's Toyota Motor Company is incorporated, a spinoff of his father's loom works. 'Toyota' takes eight brush strokes to write in Japanese, a lucky number.
29: Gottlieb Daimler patents the Reitwagen, built with Wilhelm Maybach in a garden shed at Cannstatt: the first gasoline motorcycle. Its half-horsepower engine is good for about 7 mph.
Hurricane Katrina comes ashore near Buras, Louisiana, as a Category 3 with 125 mph winds. More than 50 levee breaches flood 80 percent of New Orleans. 1,392 people die.
30: The second Morrill Act becomes law, granting cash to the land-grant colleges. States must show race is no bar to admission or name a separate college for African Americans. The South does the latter.
The Moscow-Washington hotline goes into operation. It is a teletype circuit, never a red telephone. Washington's first test message: THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPED OVER THE LAZY DOG'S BACK 1234567890.
Discovery lifts off at 8:41 a.m. Eastern on her maiden flight, two months after an abort four seconds before launch. The crew of six deploys three communications satellites and lands September 5.
31: The Detroit News station 8MK, on the air daily since August 20, broadcasts returns from that day's primary election. Now WWJ, it is believed to be the first station to broadcast news regularly.
